findings.title: LEFT JOIN drops the month filter on expenses, inflating spent totals
findings.description: The rewritten query joins expenses to budgets only on user_id and category: `LEFT JOIN expenses e ON e.user_id = b.user_id AND e.category = b.category`. The original code computed spend via monthly_summary, which scoped expenses to the given month. The new query has no condition on e.spent_on (or any month-derived filter), so SUM(e.amount_cents) aggregates every expense ever recorded in that category for the user, not just the expenses in the requested month. This means 'spent', 'remaining', and 'over_budget' will be wrong for any user with expense history spanning more than one month — a significant behavior change despite the PR claiming 'No behavior change intended'.

findings.title: PRAGMA synchronous = OFF risks database corruption, not just lost transactions
findings.description: Setting synchronous=OFF disables SQLite's fsync waits before continuing, meaning a power loss or OS crash can leave the database file in a corrupted state (not merely missing the most recent commits) under the default rollback-journal mode. This is applied globally to every connection/write in the service, not just the report path, and is a risky durability tradeoff for a financial/expense-tracking application. NORMAL (with WAL) or leaving the default FULL would be safer choices if write latency is a concern.

findings.title: No test coverage added for the rewritten budget_status query
findings.description: The diff replaces a two-step aggregation with a single JOIN query but includes no new or updated tests. In particular, there is no test verifying that spend is scoped to the requested month, which would have caught the missing spent_on/month filter regression described above. Given this is a behavior-sensitive rewrite of a financial report, tests covering multi-month expense history and budgets with zero matching expenses (to confirm COALESCE/LEFT JOIN correctness) are needed.
